CONCLUSION
To conclude, I would first like to review the characteristics revealed about
the Hong Kong Chinese migrants’ cosmopolitan identity and home in London.
Regarding identity, analysis of the data gathered suggested that the authenticity
of Chinese food chosen, consumed or prepared has little impact on migrants’
perception and construction of their own identity; and in many cases
authenticity is a topic for lively conversation but rarely taken too seriously. Most
of those I interviewed were somewhat dismissive of overtly emotional reactions
to home foods; however in the subsequent chapter about home, it can be seen
that there is more dedication towards preserving and enacting certain practices
that create feelings of homeliness. The cosmopolitan home has also been shown
to be quite a stretchy entity that can encompass features not only from Hong
Kong, but also from friends, Mainland Chinese migrants and London Chinatown
for example as features of home.
I have discussed identity and home separately in this dissertation,
however, as mentioned in the introduction, the two are deeply interconnected
and most of the examples discussed from the data could have implications on
one or both topics. One final point to add is that they are also mutually
constructive, in that a community with practices that enable migrant identities to
form will be stronger and more bonded; and being able to construct a strong
home and home community, provides an individual with the support and peace
of mind to create an identity inwardly, amongst other Hong Kong Chinese
migrants as well as the wider community.
Assuming that cosmopolitanism is an ongoing characteristic of an
individual, such as for those that have participated in my research, it can be seen
54
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
that the qualities of cosmopolitanism change in different situations and
circumstances: cosmopolitanism in Hong Kong is demonstrated by being familiar
with and routinely enjoying foreign cuisines; in London, it is the ability to
selectively be worldly and practical in some matters, but still be sufficiently in
touch with elements from home to create a lifestyle that is able to provide an
emotional and cultural cornerstone.
Admittedly, my exploration of foodstuffs, habits and places have been
more focused on verbal transcripts of participants’ conversations and
descriptions than sensory approaches that many research projects on food seem
to favour. This may be because as a researcher from the same background, the
smells of steamed rice, frying ginger and soy sauce, and the textures of food and
practices of eating with chopsticks are all so familiar to me. I would also say that
Cantonese food is less of an assult on the senses than other cuisines that might
feature spiciness, sourness, deep-frying and contrasting temperatures, just to
name a few examples. However, while it may be more difficult to articulate
appreciation of subtle and familiar flavours, the element of shared experience of
these flavours is centrally important to the role of Chinese food in creating
bonding and feelings of community amongst migrants from Hong Kong.
This dissertation covers a niche topic within a small community with
specific characteristics in terms of ethnicity, age, background and cultural and
economic resources. I hope that it is able to contribute to a deeper understanding
on the Chinese as a migrant group in the UK; and also to create interest in young
migrant communities that would appear to be increasingly seamlessly integrated
into their host populations, yet come from very diverse backgrounds and are still
forging lifestyles that retain links to their places of origin. It is important to be
55
© 2026 steflai.github.io - All Rights Reserved.
able to have insight into groups and communities that are seen as non-
problematic as they are important for the smooth functioning of a many-faceted
society, and in some cases may also become examples for solving issues among
other comparable communities. With regards to methods, those used in this
dissertation show that an open-ended and descriptive approach is able to bring
out themes and characteristics in a community that is a relatively new area of
research.
There is a Chinese saying ‘民以食為天’ (man ji sik wai tin), which
translates literally as: to the people, food is regarded as the sky. This reflects the
importance placed on food not just as sustenance, but also in people’s social,
emotional and cultural lives. While food may only be one facet of migrants’
lifestyles, it is undoubtedly one that is most frequently practised, shareable,
enjoyable and customisable of everyday life, and therefore not only very
insightful but also satisfying subject to study.
